# [The Coolest TanStack Feature](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LyKOB_xNXEY)

**Visibility**: Public
**Uploaded by**: [Josef Bender](https://www.youtube.com/@josefbender)
**Uploaded at**: 2025-11-15
**Published at**: 
**Length**: 07:41
**Views**: 7664
**Likes**: 314
**Category**: Science & Technology

## Description

```
TanStack Router and Start have a neat little feature I was sleeping on...

Let's talk about View Transitions and how to use them!

🔗 Links
Code: https://github.com/youssefbenlemlih/tanstack-view-transitions/
Newsletter: https://tanstackweekly.com

💼 Business Inquiries (e.g. Sponsorships, Consulting)
mail@youssefbee.com
```

## Transcript

If you have been using Tanak start or
TAC router in your projects, then this
video is for you. So, there's one
feature that I have been sleeping on and
once that I figured out, I decided to
just make this video because I can't
just keep it to myself and that is
[clears throat] view transitions. Now,
I'm sure you already heard of view
transitions, but in Tanstack Router,
they're actually really cool to use. So,
this is, for example, an application
that I built just for the view
transitions. You have a homepage, a
blog, and an about page. And when you
navigate from one page to another, you
have this transition between the pages.
The beautiful thing about this, well,
first of all, it's all CSS. So there is
no frame motion, no JavaScript library
that needs to be loaded for this
animation to be active. So very SEO
friendly. You don't have to worry about
client or server code. And the second
thing is that if we take a look at the
blog page, for example, if you're coming
from the about page and you click on
blog, the blog page itself is going to
slide from the left. And if you're
coming from the homepage, this is going
to slide from the right, which means you
can do some really interesting effects
depending on where you're coming from
and where you're going to. A lot of cool
stuff. Let me show you how the code
looks like. I'm also going to put this
code on GitHub, of course, if you want
to just uh clone it or copy paste it to
your project. And before we get started,
I just wanted to mention that I have
started a new newsletter and it's called
Tanstack Weekly. As the name suggests,
this is just a newsletter for keeping up
with Tanstack because the Tanstack
libraries just get too many updates and
if you're not on Twitter the whole time,
you're just going to miss on all of
that. I have just published the first
issue today actually. So if you miss it,
I'm also going to put the link to that.
Otherwise, you can also just subscribe
to the newsletter. It's free. Now, let's
get to the code. All right. So, this is
the project that we're working with. Let
me open up the files. And here we have
our source/outes
folder. This is where all our pages are
defined. And this is very
straightforward since we're using
file-based routing. So, we have the
index page. This is basically the
homepage. This is what is shown when the
homepage is clicked. Then we have the
about page. And then we also have a blog
page. So, for the blog page, this is a
folder. And inside of it we have the
index file. And here we are showing the
title and the blog entries. And here we
are using this link component. And this
is coming of course from Tanstack React
router. Then inside our slug page, we
are also searching for the blog entry
here. This is actually not that relevant
right now for this example, but you also
just show the blog content. There's a
link back to the blog. First thing we
need to do to work with view
transitions. Well, you have to define
which part of the screen or your page
you actually want to transition. And for
that, let's go to our root layout. So,
root is encapsulating the whole
application. And here you can see we
have this main tag. And inside of this,
we also have a bit of padding. We have
min minimum height of the screen. And
then there is this specific CSS property
view transition name main content. We're
going to come back to this right away.
But what we are defining here is which
part of the screen we want to transition
because if you take a look at up here,
we also have a header component. And
inside the header, we have our
navigation. So we don't want the
navigation bar to also slide left and
right. We just want the content of the
website. Great. Next thing, let's move
on to our CSS file and define some
transitions. Of course, in this code
example, I have already done this
offscreen. Uh this is pretty tedious to
do to try to code from scratch right
here. But you can just define some
transitions. And here we have the first
transition, which is slide left. Inside
this transition, we're going to have two
elements. We have the old element and
then the new element. So the old element
is the page that you're coming from and
the new one is the one that you're
navigating to. And here we can just
define how you want to animate it. For
example, here we have the slide out
left. And here we are translating X from
zero to minus 100. And we are also
setting the opacity to zero. And this is
the place where you get to be honestly
just super creative. The sky is the
limit. You can add some blur, you can do
some scaling, some rotation, maybe add
some cropping. Um really you can just
get creative. You can implement
basically anything you want here. And
this is one of the transitions. We have
transition to the left which is called
slide left. We also have the same one
for sliding to the right. I tried to
just use two transitions. And this is
actually also the code example coming
from tan stack that I have just adjusted
a little bit. So now that you have
defined your transitions, it's time to
actually use them. And this is where
tensac router really shines because the
transitions in tensac router are super
easy to implement. If you take a look at
the official documentation in the react
page, you're going to see that view
transitions is also there. But the API
is a bit cumbersome to work with and
it's definitely not as easy as it is
here. So in order to transition from one
page to another, you should simply pass
some parameters to your link component.
And let me show you how it is. So if you
go to our navigation component and this
is the header component. You're going to
see that we have the links and here we
have for example the link to the home
and we can just define which transitions
we want to have and here we are just
sliding right. So we're always sliding
from the right side. And then on the
other extreme we have the link going to
about. And here this is the opposite. So
we're always sliding from the left. And
where this gets really interesting is
when we're talking about the middle
button, which is the blog. If you can
remember, if you are coming from about
page to the blog, the blog appears from
the left. And if you're coming from the
homepage to the blog, you're
transitioning from the right. And this
is super easy to implement. Here in the
view transition prop, instead of
providing an array, we can actually
provide a function. And this function
gets a lot of very useful parameters.
And here we are using the parameter from
location. And we are checking where are
we actually coming from. Are we coming
from the homepage? Then we're going to
slide from the left. Otherwise slide
from the right. And if we control-click
from location and you're going to see
these are the properties that we are
working with. Right now, for example, I
have a small bug because if you click on
a blog post and then you click back on
the blog, you're going to slide again
from the right. We don't want that. So,
let's go back here and fix it. And here
we can add another check. So, if we are
coming from /about and this is, as you
can see here, type safe. So, when I
start writing, it's directly suggested
to me. Then, we're going to slide from
the right. And otherwise, I'm just going
to provide an empty array. So, if you're
coming from the homepage, slide left.
Otherwise, if you're coming from the
about page, slide right. Otherwise, I
don't want to slide at all. Now, if you
come back to the example, when you go to
the blog and you come back, we're not
animating anything. You can maybe
animate from the bottom. It's actually
good idea. Maybe I should have done that
for this video. Anyway, I think you get
the idea. Thanks for taking time to
watching my video. If you have enjoyed
it, please check out the newsletter and
check out my previous videos as well.
Thanks for watching and as always, see
you in the next

import { useRouter, Outlet, AnyRoute, useMatch } from '@tanstack/react-router';
import { motion, MotionProps } from 'motion/react';
interface TransitionProps {
initial?: MotionProps["initial"];
animate?: MotionProps["animate"];
}
interface AnimatedOutletProps {
enter: TransitionProps;
exit: TransitionProps;
transition?: MotionProps["transition"];
from: AnyRoute['id']
clone?: boolean
}
interface AnimatedOutletWrapperProps {
children: React.ReactNode
}
type TakeSnapshotFn = () => void
type Registry = Map
const AnimatedOutletContext = createContext(new Map())
function isDescendant(pathname: string, destinationPath: string) {
return pathname === '/' ||
(destinationPath.startsWith(pathname) &&
(destinationPath.length === pathname.length ||
destinationPath.charAt(pathname.length) === '/'))
}
export function AnimatedOutletWrapper({ children }: AnimatedOutletWrapperProps) {
const router = useRouter();
const registry = useRef(new Map())
useEffect(() => {
// NOTE: This should be onBeforeNavigate, but due to https://github.com/TanStack/router/issues/3920 it's not working.
// For now, we use onBeforeLoad, which runs right after onBeforeNavigate.
// See: https://github.com/TanStack/router/blob/f8015e7629307499d4d6245077ad84145b6064a7/packages/router-core/src/router.ts#L2027
const unsubscribe = router.subscribe('onBeforeLoad', ({ toLocation, pathChanged }) => {
if (pathChanged) {
const destinationPath = toLocation.pathname
// Find the outlet with the longest pathname, that is part of the destination route
let takeSnapshot: TakeSnapshotFn | null = null
let longestLength = 0
for (const [pathname, snapshotFn] of registry.current.entries()) {
if (isDescendant(pathname, destinationPath) && pathname.length > longestLength) {
longestLength = pathname.length
takeSnapshot = snapshotFn
}
}
if (takeSnapshot) {
// Take a snapshot of the deepest outlet
takeSnapshot()
}
}
});
return () => unsubscribe();
}, [router]);
return (

{children}

)
}

enter,
exit,
transition = { duration: 0.3 },
from,
clone = true

const [snapshots, setSnapshots] = useState<{ node: HTMLElement, id: number }[]>([]);
const [pathname, setPathname] = useState(null)
const outletRef = useRef(null);
const nextId = useRef(0);
const registry = useContext(AnimatedOutletContext)
useEffect(() => {
if (pathname) {
registry.set(pathname, () => {
const outletNode = outletRef.current!;
const snapshotNode = outletNode.firstChild as HTMLElement;
if (snapshotNode) {
let node = snapshotNode;
if (clone) {
node = snapshotNode.cloneNode(true) as HTMLElement;
} else {
outletNode.removeChild(snapshotNode)
}
const newSnapshot = { node, id: nextId.current++ }
setSnapshots((prevSnapshots) => [...prevSnapshots, newSnapshot]);
}
});
return () => { registry.delete(pathname) };
}
}, [registry, pathname]);

setSnapshots((prevSnapshots) =>
prevSnapshots.filter((snapshot) => snapshot.id !== id)
);
};
return (
<>
{pathname === null && }

{snapshots.map((snapshot) => (
key={snapshot.id}
className="absolute inset-0 pointer-events-none w-full h-full"
initial={exit.initial}

))}

A few things to note:
1. The wrapper and context is used so that nested AnimatedOutlets work. If you only have one (eg root level) animated outlet and don't need animation for sub routes, then this could be simplified by moving the router.subscribe() into the AnimatedOutlet itself. I actually started with that, until I noticed nested routes broke.
2. This version tracks multiple snapshots. This is so that if you navigate faster than the animations complete, it will continue animating previous animations. Without it, any older animations would stop abruptly and the component disappear. If you don't need this, the logic could be simplified to store only a single snapshot per outlet instead of maintaining a list.
3. The GetPathName component could be removed and useMatch called directly in AnimatedOutlet. Its here only to prevent AnimatedOutlet components from rendering on every route change, even if they don't need to.

# Super-Smooth Page Animations in TanStack Router Using View Transitions

## How to level up your TanStack Router apps with effortless, SEO-friendly page transitions.

[![SOVANNARO](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:64:64/1*4uB_4iWOhRo1dAqQ_WvQjg.jpeg)](https://medium.com/@sovannaro?source=post_page---byline--01bebeb75e86---------------------------------------)

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:1000/1*lSwD5NmlGMqyaqpYxB96_Q.jpeg)

TanStack View Transition

👉 [Non-members can read this for free here](https://medium.com/@sovannaro/super-smooth-page-animations-in-tanstack-router-using-view-transitions-01bebeb75e86?sk=5b0a6861c900c65c4ee449bca947e688)

If you’ve been using **TanStack Router** (formerly “Tanarouter” or “TANStack Start”) in your projects, there’s a surprisingly powerful feature you might be overlooking: **View Transitions**.

I recently rediscovered this feature and ended up building a small demo app just to play with it. The result was so good that I had to write this article — because once you see how simple and flexible these transitions are, you’ll definitely want to try them in your own projects.

## Why View Transitions Are So Good

Most page-to-page animations rely on client-side JavaScript libraries like Framer Motion. They work great, but they add bundle size, affect SEO, and sometimes complicate server-side rendering.

**View Transitions, on the other hand, are pure CSS.**

No animation library. No extra JavaScript. No client/server issues. And Google loves this because it keeps everything lightweight.

In my demo, I created three pages — **Home**, **Blog**, and **About**. When navigating between them, the content slides smoothly in from the left or right. What’s even better is that you can customize transitions based on _where the user is coming from_.

For example:

- If you go from **About → Blog**, the Blog page slides in from the left.
- If you go from **Home → Blog**, it slides in from the right.

This opens the door to all kinds of creative, contextual animations.

## Setting Up the Project Structure

My demo uses **file-based routing**, so the project layout looks like this:

```
src/routes/
  ├─ index.tsx        // Home
  ├─ about.tsx        // About
  └─ blog/
       ├─ index.tsx   // Blog listing
       └─ $slug.tsx   // Blog details
```

Each page is a normal component, and I use TanStack Router’s `<Link>` component for navigation.

## Step 1: Define What Should Animate

Before adding animations, you need to tell the browser **which part of the UI** is allowed to transition.

In my root layout, I wrap the main content in a container like this:

```
<main style={{ viewTransitionName: 'main-content' }}>
  {/* page content */}
</main>
```

This ensures the header (with the navigation menu) stays fixed, while only the content area animates.

## Step 2: Create the CSS Animations

Next, I defined a couple of transitions in my CSS — one for sliding left and one for sliding right.

## Get SOVANNARO’s stories in your inbox

Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.

Subscribe

Subscribe

Remember me for faster sign in

Here’s the general idea:

```
@keyframes slide-out-left {
  from { transform: translateX(0); opacity: 1; }
  to   { transform: translateX(-100%); opacity: 0; }
}
```

```
@keyframes slide-in-right {
  from { transform: translateX(100%); opacity: 0; }
  to   { transform: translateX(0); opacity: 1; }
}
```

And then you tie those animations to the browser’s View Transition API:

```
::view-transition-old(main-content) {
  animation: slide-out-left 0.35s ease;
}
```

```
::view-transition-new(main-content) {
  animation: slide-in-right 0.35s ease;
}
```

You can get extremely creative here — blur, scale, rotate, crop — anything CSS can animate, you can use.

## Step 3: Add Transitions to TanStack Router Links

This is where TanStack Router really shines. Adding animations to navigation is as simple as passing a `viewTransition` prop to your `<Link>` component.

## A basic example:

```
<Link to="/" viewTransition={['slide-right']}>Home</Link>
```

## But here’s the cool part — dynamic transitions

For my Blog link, I wanted different animations depending on where the user was coming from. TanStack Router lets you pass a **function** instead of a static value:

```
<Link
  to="/blog"
  viewTransition={({ from }) => {
    if (from.pathname === '/')       return ['slide-left'];
    if (from.pathname === '/about')  return ['slide-right'];
    return [];
  }}
>
  Blog
</Link>
```

So now the Blog page animates:

- **From left** when coming from Home
- **From right** when coming from About
- **No animation** when returning from a blog post to the blog list (to avoid awkward sliding)

This tiny function gives you full control over route-to-route transitions.

## The Result

With just a bit of CSS and a few lines in your navigation links, you get silky-smooth transitions that feel like a polished, native app — without any animation libraries or heavy client-side code.

It’s simple, clean, SEO-friendly, and incredibly flexible.

## Final Thoughts

If you’re using TanStack Router and haven’t tried View Transitions yet, you’re absolutely missing out. They’re easy to implement and add a delightful touch to any app.

I’ll be sharing the full example on GitHub so you can clone it or copy the pieces you need.

And if you’re a fan of TanStack in general, consider following the project updates. These libraries move _fast_, and it’s easy to miss some of the coolest new features.

Happy coding — and enjoy those buttery-smooth transitions! 🚀
